title: Wizard's Office permits: making them work for you
notice: Synthetic demo material. Invented document; no real meeting, publication, email or call occurred.

blocks.text: Hello everyone, and welcome. This is Rowan Bell, community manager for the Emerald City Leadership Network. Today we're talking about navigating permits and forms from the Wizard's Office. We have three people who've actually worked on these systems, and they're here to share what they've done and answer your questions. First, Ivy Coppermore, a permits clerk who works on street-stall permits.

Thank you, Rowan. Good afternoon. I'm Ivy Coppermore, I work on the street-stall permits desk. For a long time, the application was... comprehensive. Eight pages, with sections that applied only if you were selling hot food, or if your stall had a roof, or if you were within ten yards of a Brickway crossing. People would bring in forms with whole sections left blank because they weren't sure. It took time to go through each one.

So I made a checklist. One page. At the top, it asks three questions: 'Are you selling food?' 'Will your stall have a roof or walls?' 'Is your location within ten yards of a Brickway crossing?' Based on your answers, it tells you exactly which sections of the full form you need to fill out. It lists the documents you'll need to bring—proof of your market association membership, your supplier's license if it's food, that sort of thing. I keep a stack by my window. People take one, and when they come back, they have the right things. It's reduced the number of incomplete applications I get by about half, I'd say. It's just a piece of paper, but it helps them start in the right place.
That's a great example, Ivy. Thank you. Next is Marcus Wren from the South Meadow tenant advice desk. Marcus?

Hello. Yes. My work is with the tenant repair request form for South Meadow properties. The old form was a grid of small boxes: 'Nature of defect,' 'Location,' 'Date first observed.' Very bare. Tenants, especially older tenants or those for whom Munchkin isn't a first language, would often leave boxes blank or write something like 'broken' in the 'Location' field. It led to a lot of call-backs from the repair counter.

I redesigned it. The new form has the same boxes, but beside each one is a worked example in a light grey ink. Next to 'Nature of defect,' it says, 'e.g., kitchen tap drips constantly, not just a slow leak.' Next to 'Location,' it says, 'e.g., second-floor flat, rear kitchen, under the east window.' I tested it with a few tenants who'd had trouble before. One said, 'Oh, so you want the exact spot.' That was the point. I took the final version to the repair counter clerks, and they agreed to use it. Now, when a form comes in, the counter staff have a much clearer idea of what's needed and where to send the crew. It's made their sorting time quicker.
Having an example makes the expectation clear. Our last speaker is Jago Cloverley, a planning officer.

Good afternoon. I'm Jago Cloverley. My area is planning applications for small domestic extensions—a porch, a bay window, a shed in the garden beyond the standard size. People would spend weeks drawing up plans, only to submit them and be told they needed a boundary agreement from a neighbor, or that the height was non-compliant for their street. It was frustrating for everyone.

We've started offering a fifteen-minute pre-application chat. It's not a formal meeting, it's not minuted. They can come in, or we can talk on the telephone. They describe what they're thinking of building, and I can say, 'Right, for that, you'll need a scaled plan showing the distance to the property line,' or 'That height is fine, but you should check the roof material with the Gillikin Growers' association if it's slate.' It signposts the next steps. It doesn't guarantee approval, but it prevents the most common reasons for an immediate return. We've been doing this since early spring. The feedback has been that it saves people a lot of guesswork.

Thank you, Jago. Now we have time for questions from everyone listening. Please use the question function. I'll read the first one. This is for Ivy: 'Is the checklist available for us to see before coming in?'

Not yet. It's only at my desk, window four, in the permits hall. I have raised the idea of putting a copy on the public noticeboard in the hall's entrance, or perhaps having the Reading Room Network distribute it. But for now, it's physical, and it's at my window.
A question for Marcus: 'Have the counter clerks had any pushback on the new form?'

A little, at the very start. One clerk said the form looked more intimidating because there was more text on the page. But after a week, she said she was spending less time deciphering requests, so she changed her mind. The main pushback is from some of the older road crew supervisors who are used to the old brief notes. But they're adapting.
Jago, a question for you: 'How do we book one of these pre-application chats?'

You call the main planning desk and ask for one. Specify it's for a small domestic extension. They'll book a time with one of the officers. It's best to have a rough sketch or some notes about what you're proposing when you call, so they can schedule enough time.
Another for Ivy: 'Does your checklist cover permits for the festival stalls on the Great Square?'

No. That's a separate process run by the Festival Committee. My checklist is for the weekly street-stall permits on designated market lanes. The Festival Committee has its own liaison in the Wizard's Office. You'd need to speak to them.
We have time for one more. Marcus, 'Would the example form work for other kinds of requests, like noise complaints?'

I think the principle would. For a noise complaint, an example like 'e.g., hammering from flat above, daily from 7am, not just general noise' would guide someone to be specific. I haven't adapted it for that, but the idea is transferable.

Thank you all. That's all we have time for. My thanks to Ivy, Marcus, and Jago for their concrete examples. The recording and notes will be available in the network library by the end of the week. Goodbye.
